text: Once we had all made it safely to shore, we found out the island was called Malta.
The islanders showed us unusual kindness. They lit a bonfire and welcomed all of us, since it had started to rain and the air had turned cold.
Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire when the heat drove out a viper, which fastened itself onto his hand.
When the islanders saw the snake hanging from his hand, they said to each other, This man must be a murderer. Even though he escaped the sea, justice hasn't let him live.
But Paul shook the snake off into the fire and suffered no harm at all.
They kept expecting him to swell up or suddenly drop dead, but after watching a long while and seeing nothing wrong happen to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god.
Nearby were estates belonging to Publius, the chief official of the island, who welcomed us and hosted us warmly for three days.
Publius's father happened to be sick in bed with fever and dysentery. Paul went in, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.
After that, the rest of the sick people on the island came and were healed as well.
They honored us with many gifts, and when it was time to sail, they loaded us with everything we needed.
After three months we set sail in a ship that had wintered at the island, an Alexandrian ship with the Twin Gods as its figurehead.
We put in at Syracuse and stayed three days.
From there we sailed around and arrived at Rhegium. A day later a south wind picked up, and the next day we reached Puteoli.
There we found some believers who invited us to stay with them a week, and so we came toward Rome.
The believers there had heard we were coming and came out to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. Seeing them, Paul thanked God and took courage.
When we entered Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself with the soldier assigned to guard him.

Three days later Paul called together the local Jewish leaders. When they had gathered he said to them, Brothers, though I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our ancestors, I was arrested in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans.
After questioning me they wanted to let me go, since there was no charge against me deserving death.
But when the Jews objected, I was forced to appeal to Caesar - not that I had any accusation to bring against my own people.
That is why I asked to see you and speak with you, since it is for the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.
They replied, We haven't received any letters from Judea about you, and none of our fellow Jews who've come here have reported or said anything bad about you.
But we want to hear from you what you believe, since as far as this sect goes, we know people everywhere speak against it.

So they set a day and came to his lodging in even greater numbers. From morning until evening he laid out his case, testifying about the kingdom of God and trying to persuade them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets.
Some were convinced by what he said, while others refused to believe.
Unable to agree among themselves, they began leaving after Paul made one last statement: The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through the prophet Isaiah to your ancestors,
saying, Go to this people and say, You will keep hearing but never understand, and keep looking but never perceive.

For this people's heart has grown dull, their ears are hard of hearing, and they've closed their eyes - otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn back so I could heal them.
So let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles - and they will listen.
[After he said this, the Jews left, arguing a great deal among themselves.]
Paul stayed two full years in a rented place of his own, welcoming everyone who came to see him,
preaching the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, quite openly and without hindrance.
